source: And jolly enough were the sights and the sounds that came bearing down before the wind, some few weeks after Ahab’s harpoon had been welded.

It was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just wedged in her last cask of oil, and bolted down her bursting hatches; and now, in glad holiday apparel, was joyously, though somewhat vain-gloriously, sailing round among the widely-separated ships on the ground, previous to pointing her prow for home.

The three men at her mast-head wore long streamers of narrow red bunting at their hats; from the stern, a whale-boat was suspended, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was seen the long lower jaw of the last whale they had slain. Signals, ensigns, and jacks of all colours were flying from her rigging, on every side. Sideways lashed in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above which, in her top-mast cross-trees, you saw slender breakers of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck was a brazen lamp.

As was afterwards learned, the Bachelor had met with the most surprising success; all the more wonderful, for that while cruising in the same seas numerous other vessels had gone entire months without securing a single fish. Not only had barrels of beef and bread been given away to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but additional supplemental casks had been bartered for, from the ships she had met; and these were stowed along the deck, and in the captain’s and officers’ state-rooms. Even the cabin table itself had been knocked into kindling-wood; and the cabin mess dined off the broad head of an oil-butt, lashed down to the floor for a centrepiece. In the forecastle, the sailors had actually caulked and pitched their chests, and filled them; it was humorously added, that the cook had clapped a head on his largest boiler, and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare coffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooneers had headed the sockets of their irons and filled them; that indeed everything was filled with sperm, except the captain’s pantaloons pockets, and those he reserved to thrust his hands into, in self-complacent testimony of his entire satisfaction.

As this glad ship of good luck bore down upon the moody Pequod, the barbarian sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle; and drawing still nearer, a crowd of her men were seen standing round her huge try-pots, which, covered with the parchment-like poke or stomach skin of the black fish, gave forth a loud roar to every stroke of the clenched hands of the crew. On the quarter-deck, the mates and harpooneers were dancing with the olive-hued girls who had eloped with them from the Polynesian Isles; while suspended in an ornamented boat, firmly secured aloft between the foremast and mainmast, three Long Island negroes, with glittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory, were presiding over the hilarious jig. Meanwhile, others of the ship’s company were tumultuously busy at the masonry of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been removed. You would have almost thought they were pulling down the cursed Bastille, such wild cries they raised, as the now useless brick and mortar were being hurled into the sea.

Lord and master over all this scene, the captain stood erect on the ship’s elevated quarter-deck, so that the whole rejoicing drama was full before him, and seemed merely contrived for his own individual diversion.

And Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black, with a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other’s wakes—one all jubilations for things passed, the other all forebodings as to things to come—their two captains in themselves impersonated the whole striking contrast of the scene.
“Come aboard, come aboard!” cried the gay Bachelor’s commander, lifting a glass and a bottle in the air.
“Hast seen the White Whale?” gritted Ahab in reply.
“No; only heard of him; but don’t believe in him at all,” said the other good-humoredly. “Come aboard!”
“Thou art too damned jolly. Sail on. Hast lost any men?”

“Not enough to speak of—two islanders, that’s all;—but come aboard, old hearty, come along. I’ll soon take that black from your brow. Come along, will ye (merry’s the play); a full ship and homeward-bound.”

“How wondrous familiar is a fool!” muttered Ahab; then aloud, “Thou art a full ship and homeward bound, thou sayst; well, then, call me an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go thy ways, and I will mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!”

And thus, while the one ship went cheerily before the breeze, the other stubbornly fought against it; and so the two vessels parted; the crew of the Pequod looking with grave, lingering glances towards the receding Bachelor; but the Bachelor’s men never heeding their gaze for the lively revelry they were in. And as Ahab, leaning over the taffrail, eyed the homeward-bound craft, he took from his pocket a small vial of sand, and then looking from the ship to the vial, seemed thereby bringing two remote associations together, for that vial was filled with Nantucket soundings.

modern_en.title: Chapter 115 — The Pequod Meets The Bachelor
paragraphs: And jolly enough they were, the sights and sounds that came sweeping down before the wind a few weeks after Ahab's harpoon had been welded.

It was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just squeezed in her last cask of oil and bolted down her bulging hatches. Now, decked out in cheerful holiday finery, she was sailing joyfully — if a little boastfully — around among the widely scattered ships on the cruising ground before turning her prow for home.

The three men at her mastheads wore long streamers of narrow red bunting on their hats; from the stern a whaleboat was hung, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was the long lower jaw of the last whale they had killed. Signals, ensigns and jacks of all colors were flying from her rigging on every side. Lashed sideways in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above them, in her topmast crosstrees, you saw slender breakers (small casks) of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast, was a brass lamp.

It was learned afterward that the Bachelor had had the most astonishing success — all the more remarkable because many other ships cruising the same seas had gone whole months without taking a single fish. She had not only given away barrels of beef and bread to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but had also traded for extra casks from the ships she met, and these were stowed along the deck and in the captain's and officers' staterooms. Even the cabin table had been broken up for kindling, and those who ate in the cabin took their meals off the broad head of an oil-butt lashed to the floor as a centerpiece. In the forecastle, the sailors had actually caulked and tarred their sea chests and filled them. It was added, as a joke, that the cook had fitted a lid on his largest boiler and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare coffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooners had capped the sockets of their irons and filled them; that in fact everything was filled with sperm except the captain's trouser pockets, and those he kept free to thrust his hands into, as smug evidence of his complete satisfaction.

As this happy ship of good fortune bore down on the gloomy Pequod, the barbaric boom of enormous drums came from her forecastle. As she came closer still, a crowd of her men could be seen standing around her huge try-pots, which had been covered with the parchment-like poke, or stomach skin, of the black fish, and which roared loudly at every blow of the crew's clenched fists. On the quarter-deck the mates and harpooners were dancing with the olive-skinned girls who had run off with them from the Polynesian Isles, while three Long Island negroes, perched in a decorated boat hung high and firmly secured between the foremast and mainmast, led the riotous jig with glittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory. Meanwhile others of the crew were noisily busy tearing apart the brickwork of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been taken out. You would almost have thought they were pulling down the cursed Bastille, such wild cries they let out as the now useless brick and mortar went hurtling into the sea.

Lord and master of the whole scene, the captain stood upright on the ship's raised quarter-deck, where the entire joyful spectacle played out in full view before him, and seemed to have been staged solely for his own amusement.

And Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black, with a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other's wakes — one all celebrations for things past, the other all forebodings for things to come — their two captains in themselves embodied the whole striking contrast of the scene.
"Come aboard, come aboard!" cried the gay Bachelor's commander, lifting a glass and a bottle in the air.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" gritted Ahab in reply.
"No; only heard of him; but don't believe in him at all," said the other good-humoredly. "Come aboard!"
"You are too damned jolly. Sail on. Have you lost any men?"

"Not enough to speak of — two islanders, that's all; but come aboard, old hearty, come along. I'll soon take that black from your brow. Come along, will you — merry's the play — a full ship and homeward-bound."

"How wondrously familiar a fool is!" muttered Ahab; then aloud: "You are a full ship and homeward-bound, you say; well, then, call me an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go your ways, and I will mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!"

So, while one ship ran cheerfully before the breeze, the other fought stubbornly against it, and the two vessels parted. The Pequod's crew watched the retreating Bachelor with grave, lingering looks, but the Bachelor's men, caught up in their lively celebration, paid no attention to their gaze. And as Ahab leaned over the taffrail and watched the homeward-bound ship, he took a small vial of sand from his pocket; then, looking from the ship to the vial, he seemed to be bringing two distant associations together, for that vial held Nantucket soundings.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 115 — Pequod møder The Bachelor
paragraphs: Og glade nok var de, de syn og lyde, der kom svævende ned med vinden nogle uger efter, at Ahabs harpun var blevet svejset.

Det var et skib fra Nantucket, Bachelor, som lige havde presset sit sidste fad olie ned og boltet sine svulmende lugeåbninger til. Nu, pyntet i glade helligdagsklæder, sejlede det fornøjet — om end lidt pralende — rundt mellem de vidt spredte skibe på fangstfeltet, før det vendte stævnen hjemad.

De tre mænd i hendes mastetoppe bar lange strømmere af smalt rødt flagdug på hattene; fra agterstavnen hang en hvalbåd med bunden i vejret; og fra bovsprydet hang den lange underkæbe af den sidste hval, de havde dræbt, som fange. Signalflag, nationsflag og gøs i alle farver vajede fra hendes rigning til alle sider. Surret på tværs i hver af hendes tre kurvetoppe lå to tønder kaskelotolie; over dem, i mærsets tværtræer, så man smalle småtønder (små fade) med den samme dyrebare væske; og naglet til stormastens knop, kappen allerøverst på stormasten, sad en messinglampe.

Det fik man senere at vide, at Bachelor havde haft en forbløffende fangst — så meget mere bemærkelsesværdig, fordi mange andre skibe, der krydsede i de samme farvande, havde været hele måneder uden at fange en eneste fisk. Hun havde ikke blot givet tønder med oksekød og brød væk for at få plads til den langt mere værdifulde kaskelotolie, men også byttet sig til ekstra fade fra de skibe, hun mødte, og de var stuvet langs dækket og i kaptajnens og officerernes kamre. Selv kahytsbordet var slået i stykker til brænde, og de, der spiste i kahytten, tog deres måltider af det brede låg på en oliefad, der var surret til gulvet som midterstykke. I mandskabsrummet havde matroserne ligefrem tættet og tjæret deres sømandskister og fyldt dem. Det blev tilføjet for sjov, at kokken havde sat et låg på sin største kedel og fyldt den; at hovmesteren havde stoppet sin ekstra kaffekande til og fyldt den; at harpunererne havde sat hætter på tyllerne på deres jern og fyldt dem; at alt faktisk var fyldt med kaskelotolie, undtagen kaptajnens bukselommer, og dem holdt han fri til at stikke hænderne i, som selvtilfreds bevis på sin fuldkomne tilfredshed.

Da dette lykkelige skib med den gode fangst holdt ned mod det dystre Pequod, lød der et barbarisk drøn af enorme trommer fra hendes mandskabsrum. Da hun kom nærmere endnu, kunne man se en flok af hendes folk stå rundt om hendes store tranbaljer, som var blevet dækket med den pergamentagtige pose, eller mavehud, fra den sorte fisk, og som buldrede højt ved hvert slag af mandskabets knyttede næver. På agterdækket dansede styrmændene og harpunererne med de olivenhudede piger, der var løbet af sted med dem fra Polynesiens øer, mens tre sorte mænd fra Long Island, siddende i en udsmykket båd, som hang højt oppe og var fastgjort mellem fokkemasten og stormasten, førte an i den vilde jig med glitrende violinbuer af hvalelfenben. Imens var andre af mandskabet højlydt travlt optaget af at rive murværket af tranværket ned, hvorfra de store gryder var blevet taget ud. Man kunne næsten have troet, at de nedrev den forbandede Bastille, sådanne vilde skrig udstødte de, mens de nu ubrugelige mursten og mørtel susede ud i havet.
Herre og mester over hele skuespillet stod kaptajnen opret på skibets hævede agterdæk, hvor hele det glade skue udspillede sig for hans øjne, og syntes at være opført alene til hans egen morskab.

Og Ahab, han stod også på sit agterdæk, laset og sort, med en stædig dysterhed; og da de to skibe krydsede hinandens kølvand — det ene fuldt af fest over det, der var sket, det andet fuldt af anelser om det, der skulle komme — var deres to kaptajner i sig selv hele scenens slående modsætning.
»Kom ombord, kom ombord!« råbte den glade Bachelors fører og løftede et glas og en flaske i vejret.
»Har De set den hvide hval?« sagde Ahab mellem tænderne som svar.
»Nej; kun hørt om ham; men jeg tror slet ikke på ham,« sagde den anden godmodigt. »Kom ombord!«
»De er alt for forbandet glad. Sejl videre. Har De mistet nogen folk?«

»Ikke noget at tale om — to øboere, det er det hele; men kom ombord, gamle ven, kom nu. Jeg skal snart tage det sorte væk fra Deres pande. Kom nu, vil De ikke — lystigt er spillet — et fuldt skib og på vej hjem.«

»Hvor forunderligt fortrolig en nar er!« mumlede Ahab; så højt: »De er et fuldt skib og på vej hjem, siger De; nå, så kald mig et tomt skib på vej ud. Så gå Deres vej, og jeg går min. Forude der! Sæt alle sejl, og hold hende op i vinden!«

Så mens det ene skib løb glad for brisen, kæmpede det andet stædigt imod den, og de to fartøjer skiltes. Pequods mandskab fulgte den svindende Bachelor med alvorlige, langvarige blikke, men Bachelors folk, fanget af deres livlige fest, ænsede ikke deres blik. Og da Ahab bøjede sig ud over hækrælingen og så efter det hjemadgående skib, tog han et lille glas med sand op af lommen; og da han så fra skibet til glasset, syntes han at bringe to fjerne forbindelser sammen, for glasset indeholdt lodsand fra Nantucket.
